question.text:
Which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)$ where $f(x) = (x-4)(x^2+3)?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
The equation is already fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $x^2 + 3 = 0$ is \[ \mathcal{D} = (0)^2 - 4(1)(3) = -12 < 0, \] which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that the function $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=4.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by plugging the value $x=0$ into the equation: \begin{align} y & = (0-4)(0^2 + 3)\\[3pt] & = (-4)(3)\\[3pt] & = -12 \end{align}

So, the curve:

  • has a $y$-intercept at the point $(0,-12),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=4,$ and

  • has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

question.text:
Given that $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x) = 3x^3 - 9x^2 + x - 3,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x-3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x-3)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x-3)$ using synthetic division: \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrr} & x^3 & x^2 &x^1 & x^0 \\ {\color{red}{3}} & 3 & -9 & 1 & -3 \\ & & 9 & 0 & 3 \\ \hline &3 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{array} \]

Therefore, \[ \dfrac{f(x)}{x-3} = 3x^2 + 1 \]

which means that \[ f(x) = (x-3)(3x^2 + 1). \]

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $3x^2 + 1=0$ is \[ \mathcal{D}= (0)^2 - 4(3)(1) = -12 < 0, \] which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x = 3.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation: \begin{align*} y & = 3(0)^3 - 9(0)^2 + 0 - 3 = -3. \end{align*}

So, the curve:

  • has a $y$-intercept at $(0,-3),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=3,$ and

  • has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

question.text:
Given that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x)=2 x^3 + 8 x^2 + 7 x + 3,$ which of the following curves is generated by $y=f(x)?$

(Note: Figures not drawn to scale)
question.explanation:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. We are told that $(x+3)$ is a factor of $f(x),$ so $(x+3)$ divides $f(x)$ with zero remainder. To begin factoring $f(x),$ we can divide it by $(x+3)$ using synthetic division: \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrr} & x^3 & x^2 &x^1 & x^0 \\ {\color{red}{-3}} & 2 & 8 & 7 & 3 \\ & & -6 & -6 & -3 \\ \hline &2 & 2 & 1 & 0 \end{array} \]

Therefore,

\[ \dfrac{f(x)}{x+3} = 2x^2 + 2x + 1 \]

which means that

\[ f(x) = (x+3)(2x^2 + 2x + 1). \]

The equation is now fully factored. Note that the discriminant of $2x^2 + 2x + 1=0$ is

\[ \mathcal{D}= (2)^2-4(2)(1) = -4 < 0, \]

which implies that the quadratic factor has no real roots. So by the zero-product rule, we deduce that $f(x)$ has a single root at $x=-3.$

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation:

\begin{align*} y &= 2 (0)^3 + 8(0)^2 + 7 (0)+ 3 = 3. \end{align*}

So, the curve:

  • has a $y$-intercept at $(0,3),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x=-3,$ and

  • has no more $x$-intercepts.

Because the leading coefficient is positive, the graph takes an inverted ${\textsf{S}}$-shape. Therefore, the graph looks as follows:

We also find the $y$-intercept of the curve by substituting the value $x=0$ into the equation: \[ y = -4(0)^3 - 12(0)^2 - 3(0) - 9 = -9 \]

So, the curve:

  • has a $y$-intercept at $(0,-9),$

  • passes through the $x$-axis at the single root $x = -3,$ and

  • has no more $x$-intercepts.
